newsitem.title: UK: No sign of compromise over N.Ireland marches.
newsitem.headline: No sign of compromise over N.Ireland marches.

text.p: Northern Ireland's Protestants and Catholics refused on Wednesday to compromise on flashpoint parades this weekend despite pleas by the British government to focus on the need for a political settlement.

After some of the worst violence in years in the wake of a Protestant parade through the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown on Sunday, Northern Ireland was counting down to this weekend's culmination of the annual "marching season".
The Protestant Orange Order in Londonderry said it would not change its plans for a march through the British province's second city on Saturday despite objections from Catholics there.
Catholic nationalists from Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road were meeting Irish Republic ministers in Dublin as part of their campaign against an Orange march past their homes on the same day.

Gerard Rice of the Lower Ormeau Concerned Community said he wanted the Irish government to support calls for the march to be diverted from the Catholic section of the road and end a situation where Protestants march because "might is right".
Nationalists in Londonderry called on business people to close their premises on the day of the march.

"In view of the brutality meted out to the people of the Garvaghy Road, and in view of the fact that an equally grim scenario is facing the residents of the Lower Ormeau Road, the overwhelming feeling is that this (Orange) demonstration should be opposed," said Donncha Mac Niallais, spokesman for Londonderry's Bogside Residents' Group.
Saturday's parade is the first by the pr-British Orange Order in Londonderry for five years. Upwards of 10,000 Orangemen are expected to take part.
"We have been marching in this city for many years. We have given no offence," an Orange official said.
The 12th of July marks the anniversary of a 1690 Protestant battle victory over an invading Catholic King and is seen by Catholics as an anachronistic and provocative display of triumphalism.
In London, Prime Minister Tony Blair pledged not to give up the search for communal peace in Northern Ireland and came out in support of his beleaguered Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam.

"I am not going to give up on Northern Ireland. I am going to carry on searching for a solution and I believe if there were true good will on all sides and a little bit of give and take and understanding a solution could be found," Blair said.
Speaking in parliament, he backed Mowlam in her attempts to avert conflict, saying she had negotiated in good faith and praising her for her "courage and determination".
Mowlam has been bitterly criticised by the Irish nationalist community for allowing the Orange Order parade to go ahead on Sunday through a Catholic area of Portadown.
Britain's Northern Ireland security minister Adam Ingram said the government was still considering ways to resolve the Ormeau Road dilemma.

"What we are looking at is ways of trying to get accommodation between those who want to march and those who are trying to resist that march," he told BBC television. "They have got to realise the implications of their actions."

Orange Order spokesmen say they have made compromises in their demands to parade along what the call the "Queen's Highway". They say the have modified the number and routes of their parades and want only to celebrate their faith in peace.
Catholic nationalist areas of Northern Ireland were calmer overnight, with isolated incidents of shooting and petrol bombing. But the threat of further violence remained firmly in evidence.
A radical Irish Republican Army splinter group, the Irish National Liberation Army, threatened to attack members of the Orange Order if it insisted on marching down the Lower Ormeau Road.
